title: When Life Doesn't Go as Planned

memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: This is the account of Terah's family line. Terah became the father of Abram, Nahor and Haran. And Haran became the father of Lot. While his father Terah was still alive, Haran died in Ur of the Chaldeans, in the land of his birth. - Gen 11:27-28 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Here is a quiet tragedy tucked into the record: "Haran died... while his father Terah was still alive." A father buried his son. Of all the sorrows in this world, few cut deeper than a parent outliving their child. Scripture states it plainly, without explanation, without softening. Grief entered this family long before God's great promises unfolded.

Notice that this loss happens right before God's call to Abram. The family that God would use to bless the world was a family marked by sorrow. Grief and God's purposes are not opposites; they often run side by side. The people God uses are not those who have escaped suffering, but those who walk with Him through it.

Notice too Haran's son, Lot, who would journey with Abram and feature in the story ahead. Out of this loss came a boy who would be swept into God's unfolding plan. God does not waste our griefs.

If you are carrying a loss today - the death of someone dear, a life that did not go as you hoped - know that God is not absent from it. He is "close to the brokenhearted" (Ps 34:18). The family of promise knew grief too. And our Saviour Himself was "a man of suffering, and familiar with pain" (Isa 53:3). Your sorrow does not disqualify you from God's purposes; He works right through it.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
- Are you carrying a grief that feels out of place in your faith?
- Can you trust that God is present and at work even in your losses?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text:
Father, You are close to the brokenhearted, and You do not waste my griefs. Meet me in my sorrow, and work Your purposes even through the losses I do not understand.
Amen.
